Female Common toads (Bufo bufo) attain a considerably larger ultimate body size than males, with field surveys documenting a maximum snout–vent length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters] for adult females. In contrast, adult males typically reach a maximum length of only 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a pronounced sexual size dimorphism that is common among bufonids and is thought to reflect fecundity selection acting on female body volume. Newly hatched larvae, which emerge from the gelatinous egg strings after a brief embryonic period, weigh a mere 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] at the moment of eclosion, a value comparable to that reported for the related North American toad Anaxyrus americanus, on which this estimate is based. The timing of hatching is strongly temperature-dependent; at a constant incubation temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], embryos complete development and hatch after approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days]. This relatively rapid embryonic phase is typical for temperate anurans breeding in early spring, when cool water temperatures nevertheless slow metabolic processes compared to those experienced by summer-breeding species.

Following hatching, the free-swimming tadpoles of Bufo bufo embark on a period of rapid growth and morphological development that culminates in metamorphosis. At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the larval period, measured from the time since birth at metamorphosis, lasts approximately 58 days . Upon completing the larval-juvenile transition, the newly metamorphosed toadlets have a total body length of about 1.3 centimeters  and a wet weight at metamorphosis of 0.35 grams . These small but fully terrestrial juveniles then disperse from the natal pond, beginning a multi-year growth phase that will eventually bring them to reproductive maturity. The duration of the larval stage is highly sensitive to thermal conditions, and the value of 58 days reflects development under controlled laboratory conditions at 15 °C; ponds in the wild that warm more rapidly can produce shorter larval periods, while cooler water bodies may extend the tadpole stage considerably.

Sexual maturity in the Common toad is attained after a prolonged juvenile period spent foraging in terrestrial habitats such as woodlands, grasslands, and gardens. Under thermal conditions typical of temperate regions, estimated at an average of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since metamorphosis at puberty is approximately 2.5 years [tp = approximately 2.5 years], which equates to roughly 912 days. At the onset of puberty, individuals typically measure around 13 centimeters [Lp = around 13 centimeters] in total length. This size threshold appears to be a critical determinant of reproductive competence, as smaller individuals rarely engage in successful amplexus or gamete production. The ultimate wet weight of adult females, estimated from length–mass allometry, can reach 417 grams [Wwi = 417 grams], a value that underscores the substantial somatic investment required to support the production of large egg clutches. Male toads, by contrast, reach a much more modest adult body mass, with an ultimate wet weight of approximately 83 grams [Wwi = approximately 83 grams] for males, reflecting their smaller skeletal frame and the reduced energetic demands of spermatogenesis relative to oogenesis.

Reproductive activity in Bufo bufo is strongly seasonal, with adults migrating to ancestral breeding ponds in early spring to engage in explosive breeding aggregations. Under the thermal regime characteristic of the breeding season, with water temperatures averaging 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females deposit a single brood of eggs per year [F_R_i = a single brood of eggs per year]. Each female produces one large, gelatinous egg string containing approximately 1,500 eggs [N_R_i = approximately 1,500 eggs]. The synchronized breeding strategy is thought to satiate aquatic predators and maximize larval survival in temporary ponds.

The Common toad is a relatively long-lived anuran, with field studies and captive records converging on a maximum lifespan of approximately 13,000 days [am = approximately 13,000 days] when maintained at an average ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], which corresponds to about 35.6 years. This exceptional longevity places Bufo bufo among the most long-lived of European amphibians, a trait that is often associated with its slow life-history pace, delayed maturation, and iteroparous breeding strategy. Old individuals frequently exhibit signs of senescence, including reduced mobility, diminished feeding efficiency, and lower reproductive output in their final years. The ability to persist for several decades is likely facilitated by the toad’s production of bufotoxin, a potent defensive compound that deters many would-be predators and reduces extrinsic mortality rates. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that large body size and a robust defensive arsenal are common correlates of extended lifespan in the genus Bufo, and the value of 13,000 days observed in Bufo bufo aligns well with this broader phylogenetic pattern, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over rapid turnover.
